newsitem.title: USA: Trade, output reports underline U.S. economy's vigor.
newsitem.headline: Trade, output reports underline U.S. economy's vigor.

text.p: Strong overseas trade and brisk manufacturing activity, reported separately on Friday by the Commerce Department and the Federal Reserve, highlighted the economy's vigour as 1996 ended on an upbeat note.

The Commerce Department said record exports held growth in the November trade deficit to 4.9 percent as the shortfall between exports and imports rose to $8.4 billion, well below the red-ink total that was anticipated.
The Fed said national industrial output grew a stronger-than-expected 0.8 percent in December, the same as in November, as businesses operated at their fastest rates in more than a year.
However, the 83.8 percent operating rate -- up from 83.4 percent in November and the highest since 83.9 percent in August 1995 -- was seen by some analysts as a red flag for inflation.
They said it boosted odds the central bank might raise interest rates sometime in the current quarter to cool the pace, although probably not at its next policy-setting session on Feb. 4-5.
"The level itself is still not troublesome," said Peter D'Antonio, an economist with Citicorp Global Finance N.A. in New York. "But the direction and the speed at which we jumped up is troublesome."
The overall picture was of a still-robust economy entering 1997 after 6-3/4 years of unbroken growth -- since the end of the last recession in March 1991.

"The economy does seem to have gone into another re-acceleration mode," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago. "We've had a solid rebound from the third-quarter's small slowdown."

Analysts have been steadily ratcheting up their estimates of fourth-quarter economic performance as signs mount that a slim 2 percent annual rate of growth posted in the third quarter will be handily surpassed.
"This is a hot economy, it is cooking," said economist Allen Sinai of Primark Decision Economics in New York. "The production side is responding to strong sales in the fourth quarter."
Manufacturing output jumped 1.1 percent in December, after a 0.7 percent November rise, with strong production of consumer goods and business equipment.
Mining companies raised production by 1.2 percent after a 0.6 percent November gain.
Only utilities -- held back by unseasonably mild weather -- posted a 3.3 percent output drop in December following a 2.3 percent jump in November.

"The gain in industrial production ... indicates that investment will continue to be robust in 1997," said Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, adding that spending was particularly heavy for new computers.
Trade also brightened in November, in significant part because of a major improvement in the balance of business with Asian dynamos China and Japan. But oil imports also fell.
Total November exports rose 0.3 percent to a record $71.97 billion while imports increased 0.8 percent to $80.37 billion.
The deficit with China plunged 38.8 percent to $3 billion in November -- the first monthly decline in seven months -- while the shortfall with Japan shrank 12.9 percent to $4.32 billion.

It was the smallest monthly deficit with China since April, when the gap was $2.3 billion. The department said the cumulative deficit of $43.4 billion in trade with Japan for the first 11 months of 1996 was the lowest for that period since 1991.

The smaller China deficit apparently reflected the fact that merchants already had stocked up for Christmas, as imports of toys and clothing were down sharply from October. But exports to China also were at record levels, with the biggest gains in sales of soybeans and electrical machinery.
